query: For a selected high-entropy alloy whose superconducting behavior remains uncharacterized, what governs whether and how superconductivity emerges in the low-temperature test regime, and why? Propose one testable mechanistic hypothesis, a controlled comparison with the starting state, the observations expected relative to that baseline, the limits over which the hypothesis should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the selected high-entropy alloy, superconductivity emerges when a suitable level of chemical disorder (i.e. high configurational entropy) tunes the electron–phonon coupling by broadening the local vibrational spectrum. This enhanced coupling (despite the system being in the dirty limit) stabilizes an isotropic s‐wave superconducting state at low temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-synthesized, single-phase high-entropy alloy with moderate configurational disorder and a controlled crystal structure (e.g., body-centered cubic) that has not yet demonstrated clear superconductivity in the low-temperature regime.
generation.intervention: Systematically modify the alloy chemistry to increase the configurational entropy (for example, by incorporating additional transition metal elements in near-equiatomic proportions) while maintaining the same crystal structure.
generation.conditions: Low-temperature tests (below about 10 K) under ambient or controlled pressure conditions, ensuring that the phase remains homogeneous (i.e., no phase separation or major structural change occurs during alloying).
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions and broadened phonon modes induced by increased chemical complexity, which in turn adjust the density of states near the Fermi level.
generation.mechanism: By increasing configurational disorder, the alloy exhibits a broader distribution of low-energy vibrational modes. These modes enhance the electron–phonon coupling necessary for Cooper pairing in an s‐wave channel even under significant disorder (dirty limit). In this scenario, a critical threshold of chemical randomness shifts the balance so that electron scattering due to disorder becomes beneficial, rather than detrimental, to superconducting pairing.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy with higher configurational entropy is expected to show a higher superconducting transition temperature (Tc) and more robust zero-resistance behavior (e.g., improved critical current density and field robustness) compared to the baseline. Observations should reveal that superconductivity either appears or is markedly enhanced with increasing disorder up to an optimal limit.
generation.baseline: The original high-entropy alloy with lower configurational entropy (or fewer alloying elements) that either barely exhibits superconductivity (with a lower Tc) or does not show a robust superconducting state under the same test conditions.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is anticipated to hold for single-phase high-entropy alloys having similar crystal structures (such as bcc or CsCl-type) and will be valid in the low-temperature regime (roughly below 10 K). If the alloy undergoes phase separation or a structural transition due to excessive alloying, the effect may not hold.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative relationship between the configurational entropy level and the superconducting parameters, such as Tc and critical fields, is not precisely known. Moreover, it is uncertain if too high a degree of disorder might lead to excessive electron scattering that could suppress superconductivity.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: (a) a baseline high-entropy alloy with lower configurational disorder and (b) a modified version with higher configurational entropy achieved by adding additional near-equiatomic elements while maintaining the same crystal structure. Characterize both sets using structural methods (XRD, TEM) to confirm phase homogeneity, then perform low-temperature (below 10 K) electrical resistivity and magnetic susceptibility measurements under identical conditions.
measurements: Temperature-dependent resistivity to determine Tc and observe zero-resistance state
Magnetic susceptibility to confirm the onset of superconductivity
Critical field measurements (Hc1 and Hc2) to assess robustness
Structural characterization (XRD/TEM) to ensure single-phase alloying and consistent crystal structure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy with increased configurational entropy does not display a higher Tc, improved critical fields, or enhanced superconducting robustness compared to the baseline sample—or if excessive disorder leads to suppression of superconductivity—the hypothesis will be falsified.

Robust zero resistance in a superconducting high-entropy alloy at pressures up to 190 GPa

Abstract: SignificanceHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) are made from multiple transition-metal elements in equimolar or near-equimolar ratios. The elements in HEAs arrange themselves randomly on the crystallographic positions of a simple lattice. In addition to their excellent mechanical properties, one HEA has been reported to display superconductivity. In this work, we report that the Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–Ti high-entropy alloy superconductor exhibits extraordinarily robust zero-resistance superconductivity under pressure up to 190.6 GPa. Evidence for isotropic s-wave superconductivity in high-entropy alloys

Abstract: AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEA) form through the random arrangement of five or more chemical elements on a crystalline lattice. Despite the significant amount of resulting compositional disorder, a subset of HEAs enters a superconducting state below critical temperatures, Tc<10 K. The superconducting properties of the known HEAs seem to suffice a Bardeen–Cooper–Schrieffer (BCS) description, but little is known about their superconducting order parameter and the microscopic role of disorder. We report on magnetic susceptibility measurements on films of the superconducting HEA (TaNb)1-x(ZrHfTi)x for characterizing the lower and upper critical fields Hc,1(T) and Hc,2(T), respectively as a function of temperature T. Our resulting analysis of the Ginzburg–Landau coherence length and penetration depth demonstrates that HEAs of this type are single-band isotropic s-wave superconductors in the dirty limit. Despite a significant difference in the elemental composition between the x=0.35 and x=0.71 films, we find that the observed Tc variations cannot be explained by disorder effects.Subject terms: Condensed-
